lesson.title: The Weak Bond That Holds DNA Together and Lets It Come Apart
lesson.summary: This section explains how hydrogen bonds form between a partially positive hydrogen atom and a nearby electronegative atom, why they are individually weak but collectively strong, and how they hold the two strands of the DNA double helix together while still allowing the strands to separate.
lesson.body:
A hydrogen bond is not a true bond in the same sense as an ionic or covalent bond, since it does not involve atoms sharing or transferring electrons directly with each other. Instead, it is an electrostatic attraction between a hydrogen atom that is already covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom, most often oxygen or nitrogen, and a second electronegative atom nearby, usually part of a different molecule or a different part of the same large molecule. This depends directly on the polar covalent bonds introduced in the previous section: when hydrogen is covalently bonded to oxygen or nitrogen, the shared electrons are pulled toward the electronegative partner, leaving the hydrogen atom with a partial positive charge. That partially positive hydrogen is then attracted to the partial negative charge sitting on an unshared pair of electrons belonging to a nearby oxygen or nitrogen atom, and this attraction is the hydrogen bond.

Individually, a single hydrogen bond is quite weak, roughly one twentieth the strength of a typical covalent bond, and it breaks and reforms constantly at normal biological temperatures as molecules jostle against one another. But hydrogen bonds rarely act alone. When many hydrogen bonds form at once along an extended structure, their combined strength becomes substantial, even though any individual bond remains temporary and easily broken. This combination of individual weakness and collective strength turns out to be exactly the right property for several of biology's most important structures.

The clearest example is the DNA double helix. Each strand of DNA is a chain of nucleotides linked by strong covalent bonds through a sugar phosphate backbone, but the two strands of the helix are held to each other not by covalent bonds but by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases. Adenine pairs with thymine through two hydrogen bonds, while guanine pairs with cytosine through three hydrogen bonds, and the specific shapes and electronegative atoms on each base determine which bases can pair with which. Across an entire gene or genome, millions of these individually weak hydrogen bonds add up to hold the two strands together with real structural stability. Yet because each bond is weak on its own, the two strands can be pulled apart locally, without breaking any covalent bonds, whenever a cell needs to read or copy its genetic information. Enzymes involved in DNA replication and gene transcription rely on precisely this property, unzipping short stretches of the double helix by breaking hydrogen bonds, then allowing the strands to reseal behind them once the enzyme has passed. A bond strong enough to hold DNA together yet weak enough to open on demand would be difficult to achieve with covalent bonding alone; hydrogen bonding solves the problem elegantly.

Hydrogen bonds also explain the folded, three dimensional shapes of proteins, where hydrogen bonds between different parts of the same amino acid chain help stabilize coiled and folded regions, and they are central to the next two sections of this chapter, water polarity and cohesion and adhesion, both of which trace directly back to the fact that water molecules can hydrogen bond extensively with one another and with other polar substances.
